content.text:
Operator
Greetings, and welcome to the Chefs' Warehouse Q1 2024 Earnings Conference Call. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to your host, Alexandros Aldous, General Counsel, Corporate Secretary, and Chief Government Relations Officer. Please proceed.
Alexandros Aldous
General Counsel, Corporate Secretary, and Chief Government Relations Officer, Chefs' Warehouse
Thank you, operator. Good morning, everyone. With me on today's call are Chris Pappas, Founder, Chairman, and CEO, and Jim Leddy, our CFO. By now, you should have access to our Q1 2024 earnings press release. It can also be found at www.chefswarehouse.com under the Investor Relations section. Throughout this conference call, we will be presenting non-GAAP financial measures, including among others, historical and estimated EBITDA and adjusted EBITDA, as well as both historical and estimated adjusted net income and adjusted earnings per share.
These measurements are not calculated in accordance with GAAP and may be calculated differently in similarly titled non-GAAP financial measures used by other companies. Quantitative reconciliations of our non-GAAP financial measures to their most directly comparable GAAP financial measures appear in today's press release.
Before we begin our formal remarks, I need to remind everyone that part of our discussion today will include forward-looking statements, including statements regarding our estimated financial performance. Such forward-looking statements are not guarantees of future performance, and therefore, you should not put undue reliance on them. These statements are subject to numerous risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from what we expect.
Some of these risks are mentioned in today's release. Others are discussed in our annual report on Form 10-K and quarterly reports on Form 10-Q, which are available on the SEC website. Today, we are going to provide a business update and go over our Q1 results in detail. Then we will open the call for questions. With that, I will turn the call over to Chris Pappas. Chris?
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Chefs' Warehouse
Thank you, Alex, and thank you all for joining our Q1 2024 earnings call. Q1 2024 business activity displayed typical seasonal cadence as revenue trends coming out of January increased steadily in February and March. Our business units, international and domestic, delivered strong new customer and placement growth during the Q1, and aggregate price inflation continued to trend in the low single-digit range.
I would like to thank all our Chefs' Warehouse teams for sales and operations to all the supporting functions for delivering a great start to 2024. As we head into the Q2 and the rest of the year, I would also like to recognize our customer and supplier partners for their support and confidence in our people, diversity, and quality of products, and our high-touch, flexible distribution platform.
A few highlights from Q1 include 8.8% organic growth in net sales. Especially, specialty sales were up 7% organically over the prior year, which was driven by unique customer growth of approximately 10.1%, placement growth of 12%, and specialty case growth of 4.6%. Organic pounds in Center of the Plate were approximately 6.2% higher than the prior year Q1.
Gross profit margins increased approximately 37 basis points. Gross margin in the specialty category was unchanged as compared to Q1 of 2023, while gross margin in the Center of the Plate category increased 19 basis points year-over-year. Excluding the impact of Hardie's, specialty gross profit margins increased approximately 58 basis points versus the prior year quarter.
Jim will provide more detail on gross profit and margins in a few minutes. As we move into the next phase of our growth, focused on harvesting the investments we have made the past few years, our teams are engaged in continual operational improvement processes across our domestic and international markets. These work streams include implementing technology-driven product selection and loading processes in our distribution centers, enhancements to our customer-facing digital platform, as well as our continued consolidation of operation and routes in key markets.
A few highlights are during the quarter, we completed the consolidation of our Foley Fish seafood facility located in Boston into our New Bedford, Massachusetts, operation. This move reduces overhead expenses and facilitates improved cross-sell opportunities with our specialty produce and Allen Brothers distribution platform in New England.
In Northern California, our project to consolidate multiple protein processing and distribution operations into our new Richmond facility continues to progress. We anticipate initiating operations during Q2 with the phased-in consolidation during H2 2024 and Q1 2025. We expect to see the majority of operational and distribution efficiencies emerge starting in 2025.
In Texas, the integration of Hardie's and our specialty operations continues to move forward. In addition to driving cross-sell opportunities and initiating improvements in operational efficiency, our teams are making progress on capacity optimization in Houston. We expect this will facilitate growth in specialty produce and protein cross-sell to customers in the greater Houston market, as well as reduce internal transfer costs going forward.
These projects, while not all inclusive, are aimed at providing our teams with a continuous and ever-evolving platform for growth and operational efficiency within the unique business model that Chefs' Warehouse provides.
To the thousands of artisan suppliers we represent and customers we serve. We are focused on continued organic growth and building on our brand as the premier marketer and distributor of specialty ingredients, produce, and value-add proteins in the region we operate. With that, I'll turn it over to Jim to discuss more detailed financial information for the quarter and an update on our liquidity. Jim?
Jim Leddy
CFO, Chefs' Warehouse
Thank you, Chris, and good morning, everyone. I'll now provide a comparison of our current quarter operating results versus the prior year quarter and provide an update on our balance sheet and liquidity. Our net sales for the quarter ended 29 March 2024 increased approximately 21.5% to $874.5 million from $719.6 million in Q1 2023. The growth in net sales was the result of an increase in organic sales of approximately 8.8%, as well as the contribution of sales from acquisitions, which added approximately 12.7% to sales growth for the quarter.
Net inflation was 2.7% in Q1, consisting of 1.2% inflation in our specialty category and inflation of 4.6% in our Center of the Plate category versus the prior-year quarter. Gross profit increased 23.4% to $209.4 million for Q1 2024 versus $169.7 million for Q1 2023. Gross profit margins increased approximately 37 basis points to 23.9%. Our procurement, sales, pricing, and operations teams delivered strong gross profit dollar growth across categories during the quarter.
Selling, general, and administrative expenses increased approximately 21.9% to $190.3 million for Q1 2024 from $156.1 million for Q1 2023. The increase was primarily due to the higher depreciation and amortization driven by acquisitions and facility investments and costs associated with compensation, including benefits, facility costs, and distribution costs to support sales growth in the current quarter. Adjusted operating expenses increased 23.6% versus the prior-year Q1. As a percentage of net sales, adjusted operating expenses were 19.3% for Q1 2024 compared to 19.1% for Q1 2023.
Operating income for Q1 2024 was $16 million compared to $11.9 million for Q1 2023. The increase in operating income was driven primarily by higher gross profit, partially offset by higher selling, general, and administrative expenses versus the prior year quarter. Income tax expense was $0.8 million for Q1 2024 compared to $0.5 million expense for Q1 2023. Our GAAP net income was $1.9 million or $0.05 per diluted share for Q1 2024 compared to net income of $1.4 million or $0.04 per diluted share for Q1 2023.
On a non-GAAP basis, we had adjusted EBITDA of $40.2 million for Q1 2024 compared to $32.8 million for the prior-year Q1. Adjusted net income was $5.9 million or $0.15 per diluted share for Q1 2024 compared to $4.6 million or $0.12 per diluted share for the prior-year Q1. Turning to the balance sheet and an update on our liquidity. At the end of Q1, we had total liquidity of $204 million, comprised of $42 million in cash and $162 million of availability under our ABL facility.
During Q1, we executed the following transactions as part of our progress towards achieving our year-end 2025 capital allocation goals of 2.5 to 3x net debt leverage and repurchasing $25 to 100 million equivalent outstanding shares. As of 29 March 2024, we repurchased $5 million of our outstanding common shares, resulting in a reduction of approximately 135,000 shares outstanding, and we repaid $6.7 million on the outstanding balance of our term loan.
In addition, during the Q1, we repriced our $270 million term loan maturing in 2029, reducing the coupon from SOFR adjusted for a credit spread plus a fixed spread of 4.75% to SOFR plus a fixed spread of 4%, lowering interest costs by 85 to 90 basis points, depending on the SOFR term selected.
As of 29 March 2024, total net debt was approximately $662 million, inclusive of all cash and cash equivalents, and net debt to adjusted EBITDA was approximately 3.3x as compared to approximately 3.4x as of Q4 2023. Turning to our full year guidance for 2024. Based on the current trends in the business, we are providing our full year financial guidance as follows.
We estimate that net sales for the full year of 2024 will be in the range of $3.64 to 3.785 billion. Gross profit to be between $867 and 902 million, and adjusted EBITDA to be between $207 and 219 million.
Please note for Q2 and Q3 of 2024, we expect both the convertible notes maturing in December of this year, and those maturing in 2028 to be diluted for reporting purposes, and therefore, we expect the fully diluted share count to be approximately 45.9 million shares for those reporting periods. For Q4 and the full year of 2024, we expect the remaining convertible notes maturing in 2028 to be dilutive, and therefore we expect the fully diluted share count to be approximately 45 million shares for Q4 of 2024, and the full year reporting periods. Thank you. At this point, we will open up to questions. Operator?
Operator
Thank you. We will now conduct a question and answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star one on your telephone keypad. A confirmation tone will indicate your line is in the question queue. You may press star two if you would like to remove your question from the queue. For participants using speaker equipment, it may be necessary to pick up your handset before pressing the star keys. Once again, that's star one to ask a question at this time. One moment while we pull for our first question. Our first question comes from Alex Slagle with Jefferies. Please proceed.
Alex Slagle
Equity Research Analyst, Jefferies
Thanks. Hey, guys. Good morning.
Jim Leddy
CFO, Chefs' Warehouse
Good morning.
Alex Slagle
Equity Research Analyst, Jefferies
Really strong gross profit. I mean, best Q1 gross margin I think we've seen in, like, five years on an apples-to-apples basis. You know, extends on the momentum you reported in the Q4. Just kind of curious if you could dig into some of the drivers behind that, and maybe what's changed, and to the degree some of that's sustainable as we look ahead.
Jim Leddy
CFO, Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. Thanks for the question, Alex. I'll start, and I'll let Chris jump in. Yeah, I mean, ever since, you know, coming out of the summer of 2023, we really focused on gross profit dollar growth and gross profit margin. As you know, as things normalized coming out of that kind of weird summer. I think the combination of our growth in digital, providing our sales reps with more tools, more data, and still maintaining that strong sales relationship, has really helped us improve margins year-over-year and just continue the momentum that we had at the end of last year.
Alex Slagle
Equity Research Analyst, Jefferies
Okay. Yeah, I mean, even on the OpEx, I mean, I know the expectation was that we'd kind of be working through some ongoing cost headwinds and more so through H1. I don't know, it's just to the degree this is in line with your expectations, what we've reported, you know, or if there's any other dynamics, kinda given what you've seen in Q1. 'Cause, I mean, even with the higher OpEx, I mean, now it's like the EBITDA margin seems to be highest I've seen, for a Q1, at least in a really long time.
Jim Leddy
CFO, Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. I mean, to your point, OpEx came in where we expected. It's a little bit higher year-over-year, but we expected that, and we built that into the guidance. That's really mainly driven by all of the facility investments that we made in the last year or two. The main one impacting H1 of this year is we don't lap the Florida rent until the summer.
We moved in the summer of last year. Some of our other facility investments, like expansion in Seattle, expansion in the Philly, and southern New Jersey market, we won't lap those rent increases until the back half of the year as well. That's driving the year-over-year. Operating expenses were right in line with what we expected.
Our ops teams did a great job during Q1, continuing what they did in Q4.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. I think, Alex, you know, just to add to what Jim said. You know, if you look back the last few years, what I think we keep saying is that, you know, we're investing in facilities, we're investing in systems, and we're investing in people. We continue to add more and more people into business development and sales. We think we have a very differentiating approach to the market, you know, than a lot of our competition. You know, we only focus on one sector, really, and we think we're the best at it.
You know, there's always gonna be a little up and down the economy, you know, but our goal is again to be the preferred partner, you know, to most of the independent restaurants and more of the high end. I think we get rewarded for it. You know, we're all at the mercy of, you know, what really happens in the economy. I think our customers are a little more insulated. You know, the more higher end, you know, consumer has a little bit more expendable income. I think our clientele, you know, maybe doesn't have as much sway as what we're seeing right now in maybe QSR.
We're really, you know, raising prices $1 or 2 is pushing away traffic. You know, we don't have that crystal ball. You know, we thought that the quarter kinda came in where we had anticipated, and obviously, we hope that continues.
Alex Slagle
Equity Research Analyst, Jefferies
Thanks. I'll pass it along to others.
Jim Leddy
CFO, Chefs' Warehouse
Thanks, Alex.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Mark Carden with UBS. Please proceed.
Mark Carden
Executive Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, UBS
Good morning. Thanks so much for taking my question. To kind of jump on that last point a little bit, you talked about your customers being a little more insulated economically. Are you guys seeing any changes at all in the competitive backdrop with respect to pricing for distributors? Do you think any segments of your customer set are facing any pressures to lower their menu prices, or is it just different for your guys overall?
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. Well, I don't know if I've ever seen restaurants lower prices, so I don't know if that's gonna happen. You know, maybe you get a longer happy hour or you know incentives like you know Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday. It all depends on which part of the country you're talking about. You know, I think the coasts are a little different than you know the middle of the country.
You know, I mean, I think we were all concerned with the massive inflation, you know, we've seen in the last four or five years, you know, what that would do for traffic.
You know, again, most of our independents are really good restaurateurs, and they'll find that, you know, that space where they can offer value for, you know, their customer trade that is more affected by price. You know, speaking to a lot of our customers going into the call, I think it's all the expectation as well during the last year or two coming out of COVID. I think there was a lot of celebratory spending. There was customers who, maybe in the past weren't regular customers that were going out and spending more money in some of the more higher-end restaurants.
Especially I think, you know, you've heard chatter about steakhouses, and it's just amazing how many more steakhouses there are today than as customers of ours than we had four or five years ago. We think that we kind of expected that to kind of tone down a little bit. I think, you know, they were blessed with a tremendous amount of growth, and I think we're going back to a more normal pace like we saw, you know, in 2018 and 2019, where, you know, maybe some of these clients were doing 300 turns a night, and they went to 500 turns over the last year or two.
Of course, nobody likes to see the turns go backwards, but I think it's a more normal pace. We would be happy with this pace for the next 20 years. Honestly, I don't know if it's ever gonna go back to what we saw coming out of COVID. Obviously, what we saw during COVID, we never wanna see again. You know, that was horrible when all our customers closed. I think we're getting back to a more normal pace, and there'll be winners and losers.
We've seen a tremendous amount of new openings, which we kind of expected, you know, that were delayed with COVID. With that, you're gonna kind of see an evening out. I think clients, customers have more choices in many neighborhoods and in many cities.
Maybe they're, you know, I think a lot of our customers are seeing that, where there is more competition for them, where maybe there wasn't four or five years ago. You know, I think we're benefiting because we're gaining, I think, more and more customers. Even though some of our older customers might be down a bit, we're gaining with more seats in similar areas, and we're getting that extra volume.
You know, we're optimistic that, you know, it's gonna find the balance. Our job obviously is to have the most compelling proposition for customers to choose us as their distribution partners and, you know, give us a large, you know, share of that purchase.
Mark Carden
Executive Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, UBS
Got it. That's helpful context. How is your Middle East business holding up amidst some of the continued turmoil in the region? Has it remained largely immune outside of some sourcing adjustments, or has it gotten any more challenging?
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Chefs' Warehouse
I think the only challenge was business, you know, was almost too good, you know. Coming out of Q4, I think, you know, again, when we chose to enter that market, you know, we did a lot of homework, and we thought it was gonna become more and more of a chosen destination from European travelers, world travelers, and a lot of the money that's in the Middle East.
The business continues to perform. I think the only major headwind we had was that big storm. If you followed, you know, over the past few weeks, they got hit with torrential downpours that kind of flooded the streets and, you know, we lost a few days of business.
you know, some of the trouble in the Red Sea as far as getting product in was a bit of a headwind. The business that management team there is first class. They continue to execute, and we're excited about the additional building that we've been adding on and building to give them more capacity, so they can meet the demand that keeps coming.
Mark Carden
Executive Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, UBS
Thanks so much, and good luck.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Chefs' Warehouse
Thank you.
Jim Leddy
CFO, Chefs' Warehouse
Thanks, Mark.
Operator
Our next question comes from Peter Saleh with BTIG. Please proceed.
Peter Saleh
Managing Director, BTIG
Great. Thanks for taking the question, and congrats on a great start to the year. I did wanna ask about the complexion of growth for this year. Your organic growth is, you know, a little over 8% here or closer to 9%, and that's well above, like, your long-term algorithm, the 4% to 6% organic growth. Can you just help us out a little bit? How do we think about this year, and how sustainable is that organic growth rate? How do we think about organic versus acquisition benefit for the balance of this year?
Jim Leddy
CFO, Chefs' Warehouse
Thanks for the question, Pete. In terms of acquired growth, the bulk of it has happened this past quarter. The two big acquisitions we did last year were Hardie's and Greenleaf from a top-line perspective. We bought Hardie's really right at the end of the Q1, and we bought Greenleaf in the middle of the Q2. It's really heavily weighted. You know, you see our acquired RAP was, you know, 12.7% this quarter. That'll decline significantly.
In terms of organic, the mid to the high point of our guidance implies about, you know, kind of in the 6%, maybe 7% organic range for the full year. It'll decline a little bit from the, you know, 8%.
Now, some of that'll depend on price, you know, what inflation does. I think we're comfortable with the guidance right now, and it kind of implies our, you know, our long-term growth algorithm from organic perspective.
Peter Saleh
Managing Director, BTIG
Great. Can you just comment a little bit on the protein market and what you're seeing currently? I think last year around this time, maybe spring and into the summer, there was some volatility that happened. What are you seeing currently? What are the expectations, I guess, at least in the medium to near term?
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. Again, you know, I would say if we were that good at predicting commodity markets, we'd be, you know, we'd own a trading floor somewhere in Bermuda. You would think it's predictable, Peter, but you know, it's always proven us that there's some underlying factors that you know, sometimes confuse the market.
You know, it's driven by retail, right? If retail slows down, especially for what we buy, which is you know, upper choice and a lot of prime, you know, you do get breaks in the prices. I think year-over-year we had a few points of inflation over last, you know, last year's Q1.
You know, we don't take major positions. You know, we've learned that there isn't a lot of upside unless the price has dropped so low that, you know, you're really comfortable to take a much larger position. I think that, you know, we go with the market. You know, if customers want to buy in and have us take a position for them, we'll do it. You know, we try to avoid that big risk of being wrong.
Jim Leddy
CFO, Chefs' Warehouse
Pete, I'll just add that, you know, while we had some year-over-year inflation, you know, prices in the protein market in Q1 kind of behaved kind of how they've behaved historically. In other words, sequentially coming out of the holiday season in Q4, you know, prices kind of declined as they normally do in Q1. Historically, you would see them start to ramp up as you're going into barbecue season in the summer. That's, you know, that's still to be determined.
Peter Saleh
Managing Director, BTIG
Understood. Thank you very much. I'll pass it along.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Chefs' Warehouse
Thanks, Pete.
Operator
The next question comes from Andrew Wolf with C.L. King. Please proceed.
Andrew Wolf
SVP and Senior Equity Research Analyst, CL King
Hi. Thank you. Good morning. Wanted to ask also sort of on the organic sales being, you know, so much stronger than your competitors and really most of the sector, the restaurants it's included. How much would you sort of say this is, you know, your core customer base just being, you know, more well-positioned, less sensitive to inflation and their consumer behavior versus, you know, you just taking share of the business either through better selling or better products and selection, or just more, you know, people going up and down the street?
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Chefs' Warehouse
You know, Andy, I think a lot is with taking share. I don't wanna sound like Rodney Dangerfield that we get no respect, you know, being smaller of all the public companies in the space. You know, we've invested a lot, you know, people that really understand our business and are, you know, follow our story. We're not a new business, you know, we're getting close to our 40th anniversary. We know the industry really well, and we've made big bets. We've invested in facilities, we're investing in technology, and we've made tremendous investments in talent, and, you know, no one's completely immune to economic cycles.
We, you know, made the investments to continue to grow and continue to protect our turf, you know. Our turf is really, you know, upscale casual to fine dining and to be the best at it. I think I hate to have a Cassandra's crystal ball prediction, but, you know, doing this now for almost 40 years, I've seen a lot of the cycles. Yes, you know, we do have a piece of our customer portfolio that they are down. You know, they are seeing negative comps.
We kind of expected that people continue to go out, and they do have a lot of choices, and we go after a huge amount of new customers every year to have that diversity of super high-end, high-end, scale casual, and emerging concepts.
You know, we went into produce. You know, I call it that's our plant-based hedge. You know, we like the business. We bought Hardie's last year to get into Texas. A great company. We're Chefs'-izing it, like we said. We're gonna add more and more products and give their sales teams more opportunities, and we call it more at-bats with customers with all the Chefs' products.
You know, our over 50,000 items that, you know, make us who we are, that come from, you know, thousands of artisan producers. I think we expect, you know, to continue to grow and outgrow, you know, most of the industry. Obviously, there'll be some headwinds in the way, but we think our investments were the right investments, and we expect to get rewarded.
Andrew Wolf
SVP and Senior Equity Research Analyst, CL King
Great. Thank you, Chris. Appreciate that. Can I just ask one other question? It's not really a follow-up. You haven't mentioned, you know, labor productivity, I think, or I didn't hear it at least. Where I know in past quarters, sounded like you felt pretty good about it. Can you just give us an update how you're feeling about, you know, hiring, training, turnover, labor productivity?
And, you know, where I think you mentioned you're gonna invest in some automated picking. I know that's longer term and sort of a separate thing, but, you know, where that fits into, I guess, your cost structure going, you know, long-term cost structure.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. It's still people, process, product. People are, you know, they're our greatest asset, and we keep investing in, you know, trying to make it a great place to work. It's always challenging. Obviously, you know, COVID was, you know, a new level of the word challenging. I think we're getting more and more productive. I think the team, especially in the new areas we've invested in, it will continue to get better. As you know, training, we've invested in more and more into training. I think you have to. You have a lot of new people coming into the industry.
You know, I would say nobody really graduates, you know, school and comes out and says, "I really wanna go into food service," right? It's not like you're looking for accountants or doctors or bankers. It's people that are, you know, we hire a lot out of the industry. In sales, you know, we have a lot of chefs that work for us that have changed careers. In a lot of the other positions, it's people that are coming in to the industry, and you have to train them, and you have to make sure that you make it a great place to work because we want them to stay. It does take years for them to get better and better at their job.
No matter how much technology you have, we are in the people business. Always a headwind, but it's what we do, and we think we do it really well, and we continue to get more productive.
Jim Leddy
CFO, Chefs' Warehouse
Andy, I'll just add that, you know, when we talk about our five-year plan and getting operating leverage, you know, gradually increasing as we, you know, as we go through the next 2-5 years. You know, a big part of that is the impact on rationalizing labor and labor costs through consolidating facilities like we're doing in Northern California.
We're doing in Florida now. We're doing in Texas, New England, consolidating routes as part of those facility consolidations. Then the tech-related process improvements are really focused on error reduction, and a lot on inventory management.
I think our operating teams and our procurement teams are doing a great job of starting that, and hopefully we get more benefit from it down the road as well.
Andrew Wolf
SVP and Senior Equity Research Analyst, CL King
Okay. Thank you. Appreciate it.
Operator
The next question comes from Kelly Bania with BMO Capital. Please proceed.
Kelly Bania
Managing Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, BMO Capital
Good morning. Thanks for taking our questions. Jim, we're starting to touch on this a little bit, but just was curious if you can update us on the pace and the cost of those facility expansions, whether it be, you know, Northern California or, some of the others that you have going on, or those coming time-wise and expense-wise on plan and any changes to that outlook for this year.
Jim Leddy
CFO, Chefs' Warehouse
No real changes to the outlook. I think, you know, we have a little bit of front-loaded CapEx, you know, in H1 as we finish our building in Northern California. We expect in a few weeks to start the phased-in consolidation of four separate facilities.
I think as we mentioned in our prepared remarks, we expect most of the cost savings and efficiencies to really emerge in 2025 because we're gonna spend the rest of this year really in a very thoughtful, phased-in consolidation, just managing the logistics and servicing the customers through that process. You know, we've finished most of the consolidation in Florida.
From an OpEx perspective, I'll just go back to what I stated earlier. Most of the impact from a year-over-year perspective is in the H1 as we lap those increased rents that we had last year. The year-over-year will, you know, we expect to get better. That's assuming, of course, top line and gross profit hold up accordingly per our guidance and per our plan.
I think, look, we'll get the bulk of the benefit, you know, really starting in the latter part of this year and then into 2025 and then into 2026. It's really setting us up for you know, the next couple of years in terms of generating operating leverage.
Kelly Bania
Managing Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, BMO Capital
Great. Thank you. Can you also just touch a little bit more on the seasonality trends that you're seeing? It sounds like the spring has really trended as expected or maybe a little bit better, but there's always a lot of moving parts in the spring. Just help us understand what you're seeing so far, and any real divergences among geographies that might be of note.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Chefs' Warehouse
Well, I think the only thing we would mention is, you know, with the early Easter, there was a little bit of noise around the last week of March and the first week of April, but with nothing like hugely material that we would necessarily call out. The rest of April started to build back to where we expected, or very close to where we expected. I don't think, you know, we see anything going into the summer. You know, hopefully we don't have the kind of volatility or significant international travel impact that we had last summer, but, you know, obviously we can't predict that right now.
I wouldn't say there's anything that we would call out right now seasonally, other than, you know, there's, you know, as we talked about earlier, there's always concerns about the macroeconomic environment that we're hearing a lot about.
Kelly Bania
Managing Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, BMO Capital
Okay, that's helpful. Just another one on the SKU count. Obviously, there's been a lot of acquisitions and expansions into new categories, but the SKUs are up to 70,000, I believe, now. What's the right number over time? How do you make sure to balance that selection and with the complexity of having more and more SKUs? Just any thoughts on that?
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. Well, the SKUs is, again, you gotta be very careful. It's a little misleading, sometimes because, you know, it's kinda like the 80-20 rule. I mean, you know, 80% of the business is in 20% of the SKUs. We run a huge just-in-time process because of our independent customer base, it puts a tremendous demand on being able to accommodate a lot of the creativity that, you know, the people that run these restaurants demand of us. I think that's one of the things that, you know, we are probably the best in the industry, 'cause we kind of understand it. You know, we've been doing it for so long.
I think as we get bigger, and we expand more territories and more categories, I think that proliferates a lot of, you know, the amount of SKUs that come through the system. It is something we focus on every day to obviously be accommodating, but also have the discipline so you don't have the waste. I think what's driving the SKU count up is we've expanded a lot of the categories. With the category expansion, you have a lot of SKUs that come in and out.
I still think that, you know, when you really look at what's in the buildings, and we do work on this every day because, you know, you have to draw the line somewhere where, you know, you have how much duplication of inventory that's very similar.
So I think category management does a great job with that and continues to work on educating the sales staff and customers that we may have what they're looking for. It might be a different label, or it might be a different pack size, but please take what we stock because bringing in new product is very expensive, right? Warehouse space continues to get very expensive. Frozen space, obviously, is very expensive today to build.
I wouldn't get too held up on, you know, the massive proliferation of SKUs.
Kelly Bania
Managing Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, BMO Capital
Great. Thank you.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Chefs' Warehouse
Thanks, Kelly.
Operator
The next question comes from Ben Klieve with Lake Street Capital. Please proceed.
Ben Klieve
Senior Research Analyst, Lake Street Capital
All right, thanks for taking my questions. A couple quick ones for me. First of all, Jim, I appreciated your comment that CapEx this year is gonna be front-loaded, Q1 as a percentage of sales to 2%. I'm hoping you can elaborate on this a bit in some way. You know, full-year CapEx expectations, perhaps your expectations for kind of the range of CapEx as a percentage of revenue. You know, just kind of some sense of how this line item is gonna play out for the balance of the year.
Jim Leddy
CFO, Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. Thanks, Ben. I think we should come in pretty close to 1%. You know, maybe it's 1.1% or 1.2% or maybe a little bit below. The bulk of our CapEx this year are two major projects, which is finishing out the Richmond, California facility I talked about earlier, which is a big project, and then our Chef Middle East expansion. The bulk of that project is happening in H1 of the year, and then we'll round out into H2 of the year. Then we have the normal kind of technology investments and maintenance CapEx.
As those two projects finish towards, you know, the end of Q3, that, you know, that back half of the year we expect to be on the lower end and the H1 of this year to be on the higher end. I think, you know, we put out our guidance of $35 to 45 million of CapEx. I expect us to stay within that range. If we land within that range, we'll be pretty close to our goal this year of close to 1% of revenue.
Ben Klieve
Senior Research Analyst, Lake Street Capital
Great. There's kind of a steep decline here throughout the year. That's perfect. Thanks, Jim. Last one for me, and I'll get back in queue. A product-specific question regarding cocoa just going parabolic this year. I know it's not a huge element of your business, but I'm just curious, you know, how effectively you guys have been able to navigate this, if this has been any issue in Q1 or so far here in Q2?
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah, I mean, it is a good topic. It's a little frightening what's happened in the cocoa market, and it's just amazing that the demand for chocolate desserts is still very high. I think we do offer a plethora of choices for customers. You know, we carry many types of different chocolate, and it's something that I look at, you know, on a weekly basis. You know, the concerns were, oh my God, people are gonna stop eating chocolate, and that just doesn't happen.
People are, you know, there is a little switching, you know, in brand, something a little bit more affordable, but our customer base continues to enjoy, you know, producing the desserts, and the demand is still there.
Ben Klieve
Senior Research Analyst, Lake Street Capital
Got it. Very helpful. All right. I appreciate you guys taking my questions. I'll get back in queue.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Chefs' Warehouse
Thanks, Ben.
Operator
The next question comes from Todd Brooks with Benchmark Company. Please proceed.
Todd Brooks
Senior Analyst and Managing Director, Benchmark Company
Hey, good morning. Thanks for taking my questions. First question, Chris, you talked about touching base with a bunch of your customers in advance of the call. I'm just wondering, we're going into a bit of the celebratory season here, Mother's Day, Father's Day, graduation, and then we obviously roll into the strongest window for, or one of the stronger windows for events across the summer. What are you hearing about those two slices of the market and the business from your customers?
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. I think that part is unchanged from what I'm hearing that you know events were booked, events are happening. Obviously, we're coming out of you know with nothing happening in COVID. We kind of expected that, you know. You know, Vegas sounds very strong. Again, the UAE sounds very strong. I think lots of weddings, lots of christenings, bar mitzvahs, graduations. I think the catering side is pretty strong. We don't hear anything that you know would cause us to think any different at this point.
Todd Brooks
Senior Analyst and Managing Director, Benchmark Company
Great. Second question. I know we don't want to crystal ball too much on inflation, but in just listening to the restaurant companies, it seems like inflation's firmed up maybe a little bit more than they expected going into the year. I know, Jim, you shared the 2.7% inflation for Q1. How are you thinking about maybe brackets around the inflationary environment as you're looking 2024, and then maybe H2 of this year?
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Chefs' Warehouse
Are you saying deflationary environment?
Todd Brooks
Senior Analyst and Managing Director, Benchmark Company
Inflationary, yes.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Chefs' Warehouse
Inflation. Yeah. Yeah. Well, protein really caused from last year over a point different. I think our specialty, you know, fresh specialty business was only about a point and a half, you know, of inflation. We've really seen that moderate. It's really, you know, the labor factor. I don't think the cost of labor is gonna go down. I think it's pretty embedded now in everybody's, you know, forecast that you're gonna have that continued high labor cost. We were worried about deflation for a while. That's why I said, are you asking about deflation or inflation? We don't see, you know, there's always something in the world.
I mean, obviously we have, you know, wars going on and, you know, we watch the cost of freight and what's happening to transport, the cost of fuel. We don't see anything really that would make us think that, you know, something drastic is gonna happen, you know, in the cost of goods and, you know, either way, deflation or inflation at this point.
Todd Brooks
Senior Analyst and Managing Director, Benchmark Company
Okay, great. Thanks. One final one. Center of the Plate pounds, very strong in the quarter, up in that 6% range. I guess, what's the complexion of that? Are you seeing, was it actually a switch back to beef with that sequential kind of stabilization that you saw, or is it other proteins that are driving that growth? Just any color you can give us there. Thanks.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah, I mean, we continue to see demand there, you know, across the board. You know, I thought with the gluten-free craze started, we wouldn't sell any pasta. We sell lots of pasta. We sell a lot of vegetables too, but we sell a tremendous amount of steak and what we think is the best hamburger in the market. We sell a tremendous amount of chicken. We're not seeing anything really, you know, change in, you know, the demand that we saw over the past few years, you know, the trends. I think it's kind of spread out. There's big diversity in menus, and people like choices.
We were talking about this the other day, you know, do we think menus are gonna shrink or many neighborhood restaurants, I mean, they're serving the same customers week in, week out. They have to continue to be creative, and they have to continue to give people a reason to come back. Obviously, there's the house favorites, but everybody likes something a little different. I think that's what independent restaurants do really well. They're constantly creative, and they're constantly making it, you know, more interesting, for their patrons to keep coming back. I think that trend continues.
Todd Brooks
Senior Analyst and Managing Director, Benchmark Company
Okay, great. Thanks, Chris.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Chefs' Warehouse
Thanks, Todd.
Operator
Thank you. At this time, I would like to turn the call back to management for closing comments.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. Well, we thank everybody for joining our call today. Chefs' Warehouse's team is hard at work, and I think their success is well-earned. We're hoping for a great next quarter, and we look forward to everybody to join our call again. Thank you very much.
Operator
Thank you. This does conclude today's teleconference. You may disconnect your lines at this time. Thank you for your participation and have a great day.
